doc.title: Gene Bertoncini interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Architecture degree and how it shapes his arranging
summary: He studied architecture, and compares planning a concert to presenting plans, arranging for guitar as a little orchestra, citing Julian Bream.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You had other interests besides music too, didn’t you? Growing up?
Yeah. I have — I like girls.

I knew that’s what you were referring to. No I have a degree in architecture. I fell in love with architecture. I used to copy the plans out of the New York Times Sunday real estate section. And I did some work in construction. My dad always — he rebuilt two homes when we were growing up and so I was always like kind of interested in the building stuff. I always thought I might be in that area. And my high school advisor said — well when I told him I liked, I also liked drafting. In those days we actually drew with pencils and T-squares. I was really upset to visit the Frank Lloyd Wright office and school in Taliesin Arizona and to see that everything was computer. Everything. They don’t use — maybe if you’re lucky they might do a sketch for you. But in those days, and that was © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
such — to have that white piece of paper and the tools to draw with, to make lines. That was very nice. I enjoyed that a lot. I still would enjoy that too.
Do you think that had any effect on — that interest — in the way you play?

Yeah. Yeah I do. I like to plan stuff. I like to — when I play a piece of music I usually arrange it and I usually think of a concept for it, and have an area where there’s improvisation. I like to think of the guitar as my little orchestra, or a big band. And I do arrangements for my big band. And I play them and I work out fairly complicated things. I was fortunate in that I fell in love with the music of — aside from jazz players — the music of Julian Bream, a great English guitarist and I heard his interpretation of the Ravel “Pavanne” and the amazing orchestra qualities that the guitar has. And so it’s really worth the effort of trying to arrange things for the guitar. So in that sense, the way an architect would present a set of plans or a colored drawing of a building to a client, I think I do the same with the music in a concert. I like to present a finished set of plans to an audience. But in the middle of it is this, just as in a big band, I went to hear Maria Schneider’s band the other night, and I heard her wonderful arrangements, and she plays, the band plays those arrangements. She writes new ones, but they play those arrangements as is, and the difference every night is the spirit of the evening, whatever happens and the sections where the guys get a chance to improvise. And that’s what I feel about the guitar, I could do. And I don’t feel like I’m cheating by playing the same arrangements. Of course, every night there’s some things you do off the top of your head, which you can’t really do with a big band.
That’s right. It gets a little unwieldy.
